claims.text: High-energy ball milling of W and Cu powders before spark-plasma sintering will reduce the void fraction of the resulting W–Cu composite.
High-energy ball milling before spark-plasma sintering will improve interfacial contact between the W and Cu phases.
The mechanically alloyed and SPS-sintered composite will have higher thermal conductivity than a W skeleton infiltrated with molten Cu.
The mechanically alloyed and SPS-sintered composite will have greater mechanical durability under fusion-relevant irradiation than a W skeleton infiltrated with molten Cu.
An inert milling atmosphere will prevent or limit oxidation during processing.
Mechanical alloying breaks up agglomerates in the W–Cu powder mixture.
Mechanical alloying increases powder surface area and contact between W and Cu.
The increased W–Cu contact produced by mechanical alloying promotes diffusion during spark-plasma sintering.
Mechanical alloying followed by spark-plasma sintering minimizes phase separation and void formation.
Reduced void formation and improved W–Cu interfacial contact improve thermal transport.
Reduced void formation and improved W–Cu interfacial contact improve mechanical durability.
The proposed composite will exhibit at least a 20% increase in thermal conductivity relative to conventional Cu infiltration into a W skeleton.
The proposed composite will have improved mechanical strength, such as flexural strength, relative to conventional Cu infiltration into a W skeleton.
The proposed composite will have fewer voids and a more uniform microstructure than the conventional infiltration baseline.
Excessive milling time or processing temperature may cause contamination or unwanted phase formation.
Extreme neutron flux or temperature may degrade the composite's performance.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome assigns the 20% threshold only to thermal conductivity and merely predicts improved mechanical strength, whereas the falsification rule can be read as requiring a 20% improvement in either thermal conductivity or mechanical strength. This makes the mechanical-strength threshold inconsistent or ambiguous.
